# Partition study hypotheses

## H1 [tentative]
Target partition depends on the categorical solvent–extractant pairing, not on matching anonymous indices. At fixed equal phase additions, at least some pairings should show repeatable differences in organic fraction. A 12-batch screen with deliberate repeats will test this; absent separation beyond stated HPLC/final-assay uncertainty, the claim will remain unresolved.

## H2 [tentative]
For a fixed pairing near equilibrium, increasing organic share should increase the fraction of the fixed initial target inventory found in organic, while changing concentration and phase_ratio. This is a phase-volume prediction, not an assumption that added aqueous liquid is the entire aqueous volume.

## H3 [tentative]
More vigorous/longer mixing should primarily affect approach to equilibrium; if low and high mixing agree within measurement uncertainty after identical settling, mixing intensity has no resolved effect over that tested range.

Plan: use pre-separation HPLC in every batch to observe both phases, then retain a declared phase, explicitly terminate, and final-assay. Pairing screens precede focused volume/mixing tests; adaptations will remain cautious because single noisy differences are not effects.

# Partition study hypotheses

## H1 [supported for screened one-factor contrasts; interaction unresolved]
At fixed additions (0.04 L solvent, 0.04 L aqueous, 0.02 L extractant) and 300 s/600 rpm mixing plus 300 s settling, material choice changes partition. With S0, pre-separation organic inventory fraction rose from 0.217 (X0; event runner-operation-0007) to 0.404 (X1; -0017), 0.291 (X2; -0027), and 0.467 (X3; -0037). With X0, changing S0 to S1/S2/S3 gave 0.392/0.310/0.429 (events -0047/-0057/-0067). These are numerical contrasts substantially larger than the declared HPLC channel noise, but each pairing is still unreplicated. Anonymous indices carry no ordered or identity meaning. Solvent–extractant interaction remains unresolved because the screen varies one factor from S0/X0 rather than crossing all pairs.

Prediction recorded before focused batches: repeats of S0/X3 and S3/X0 should remain among the higher organic fractions, whereas a failure well outside expected instrument noise would suggest process variability or an uncontrolled interaction.

## H2 [tentative]
Within S0/X3, increasing extractant volume and lowering aqueous/solvent volumes should increase phase_ratio and product_in_organic; decreasing extractant should do the converse. Because solvent addition and initial liquid contribute to real volumes, inference will use measured phase_ratio rather than equating aqueous addition with total aqueous volume.

## H3 [tentative]
Within S0/X3 and identical phase amounts, a low-mixing batch (10 s, 100 rpm) will be compared with standard mixing. Agreement within measurement/process uncertainty would only support mixing-insensitivity over those tested conditions, not prove equilibrium.

## Retention/closure check
Pre-separation HPLC reports both-phase inventory. Organic-retained final assays in batches 1–7 generally preserve the pre-separation organic fraction within sampling/noise (events -0007/-0010 through -0067/-0070), while aqueous signal falls near zero; this supports the interpretation that separation removes a phase rather than switching a sampling label. One focused batch will instead retain aqueous to test the complementary consequence.

notes.text:
# Partition study conclusions (source-stage)

## H1 [supported in screened scope; interactions unresolved]
At fixed 0.04 L solvent + 0.04 L aqueous + 0.02 L extractant and standard mixing/settling, both anonymous factors affected partition. S0/X3 replicated: pre-separation organic fractions 0.467 and 0.453 (events runner-operation-0037 and -0077). S3/X0 also replicated: 0.429 and 0.436 (-0067, -0087). These repeat agreements strengthen the earlier one-factor contrasts. Only S0 was crossed over all X and only X0 over all S, so untested pair interactions cannot be predicted from index or assumed additivity.

## H2 [supported directionally for S0/X3; simple constant-coefficient model inadequate]
Changing the recipe toward more extractant/less solvent and aqueous increased measured phase_ratio from about 0.18–0.19 in standard repeats to 0.609, and organic inventory fraction to 0.811 (event -0097). The low-extractant recipe gave phase_ratio 0.113 and organic fraction 0.307 (-0107). Direction matches the prior prediction and is far larger than declared HPLC noise. However these recipes change three additions together, so phase amount is not isolated from dilution/composition. Derived apparent concentration partition ratios D=(O/A)*(1-r)/r are approximately 3.71 and 3.99 for standard repeats, 2.60 high-extractant, and 3.50 low-extractant; thus a single constant-D law is not supported across the entire tested range. A descriptive four-point least-squares relation for standard-mixed S0/X3 is O≈0.256+0.926r, but it is not validated and should not be extrapolated.

## H3 [suggestive mixing effect; unresolved]
Low mixing (10 s, 100 rpm) at the standard S0/X3 recipe produced O=0.381 and A=0.645 (event -0117), below the two standard-mixing O replicates 0.467 and 0.453. The gap exceeds stated HPLC channel noise, suggesting incomplete approach to the standard state. Yet duration and rpm changed together and the low condition lacks replication; equilibrium, kinetics, and batch variability remain alternatives. A replicate low-mix batch or a duration-by-speed design could change this conclusion.

## Phase retention and closure [supported operationally]
Organic-retained final assays preserve organic inventory approximately while aqueous becomes near zero (e.g. -0037 to -0040; -0087 to -0090). The aqueous-retained test likewise changed phase_ratio to 0 and organic to 0, while aqueous remained 0.575 after pre-separation 0.524 (-0077 to -0080). This supports physical removal rather than a sampling switch. The aqueous difference, elevated impurity, and purity change warn that sampling/instrument/process effects prevent exact closure. No missing measurement was treated as zero.

## Predictive scope and next tests
Within S0/X3, measured phase_ratio is the safest empirical predictor of direction: larger r should generally mean more target inventory in organic, and organic retention is appropriate when that phase carries the larger desired share; aqueous retention is appropriate when the desired share is aqueous. This is not a universal material law. Blind predictions for unseen pairings should carry high uncertainty because most interactions, the initial liquid composition, time-to-equilibrium, and independent phase-volume changes remain unavailable. Priority tests would replicate low mixing, vary extractant at fixed solvent/aqueous where vessel capacity permits, and add selected crossed S/X pairs.

payload.report:
Observations

The supplied information identified four anonymous solvents (S0–S3) and four independent anonymous extractants (X0–X3), but supplied no physical-property dossier. It explicitly warned that equal indices do not imply related materials. Thus all material claims below come from the campaign rather than chemical-identity assumptions. The instrument contract supplied calibrated observable channels and approximate channel noise; it did not reveal the hidden species mapping or guarantee equilibrium.

Seven initial batches used the same reagent amount, liquid additions (0.04 L solvent, 0.04 L aqueous phase, 0.02 L extractant), mixing (300 s at 600 rpm), and settling (300 s). In this controlled screen:

• With S0, changing X0/X1/X2/X3 produced pre-separation HPLC product-in-organic signals of 0.217, 0.404, 0.291, and 0.467, respectively (batches 1–4; events runner-operation-0007, -0017, -0027, and -0037). The corresponding aqueous signals were 0.734, 0.627, 0.704, and 0.523.
• With X0, changing S0/S1/S2/S3 produced organic signals of 0.217, 0.392, 0.310, and 0.429 (batches 1 and 5–7; events -0007, -0047, -0057, and -0067).
• The higher standard-condition observations were reproducible: S0/X3 gave organic signals 0.467 and 0.453 in batches 4 and 8 (events -0037 and -0077), while S3/X0 gave 0.429 and 0.436 in batches 7 and 9 (events -0067 and -0087).

The focused S0/X3 volume experiments changed several additions together. The standard recipes had measured phase_ratio values near 0.18–0.19 and organic signals of 0.453–0.467. A recipe with 0.06 L extractant and only 0.02 L each solvent and aqueous phase gave phase_ratio 0.609, organic 0.811, and aqueous 0.200 (batch 10, event -0097). A recipe with 0.01 L extractant, 0.04 L solvent, and 0.05 L aqueous phase gave phase_ratio 0.113, organic 0.307, and aqueous 0.686 (batch 11, event -0107).

A low-mixing S0/X3 batch retained the standard liquid amounts but used 10 s at 100 rpm. It gave phase_ratio 0.195, organic 0.381, and aqueous 0.645 (batch 12, event -0117), compared with organic 0.453–0.467 and aqueous about 0.524 in the two standard-mixing repeats.

Phase-removal measurements behaved complementarily. After retaining organic, final assays generally preserved approximately the preceding organic signal while the aqueous channel became zero or nearly zero; examples include batch 4 (0.467 before separation and 0.450 in the organic-retained final assay, events -0037/-0040), batch 9 (0.436 and 0.420, events -0087/-0090), and batch 10 (0.811 and 0.792, events -0097/-0100). In batch 8, retaining aqueous instead produced final organic 0 and aqueous 0.575 after a pre-separation aqueous signal of 0.524 (events -0077/-0080). The channels do not close exactly, and the aqueous-retained final sample also showed increased impurity signal and lower purity.

Inference

1. Material pairing matters. The controlled contrasts are much larger than the declared HPLC product-channel noise, and the two selected high-organic conditions reproduced closely. Both solvent and extractant identity contribute: neither factor can be treated as a passive label. S0/X3 and S3/X0 are supported only as relatively organic-favoring pairings within the screened conditions, not as universally superior materials.

2. Phase amount strongly controls how much target is found in the organic phase. Within S0/X3, increasing the measured organic phase share was accompanied by a large rise in the organic target signal, while reducing it had the opposite effect. Phase_ratio is therefore a useful empirical predictor of direction in this local system.

3. A single invariant partition coefficient is inadequate over the whole tested range. Using the observed organic and aqueous signals with measured phase_ratio gives heuristic apparent concentration ratios of about 3.7–4.0 for the two standard S0/X3 repeats, about 3.5 for the low-extractant condition, and about 2.6 for the high-extractant condition. These differences may reflect composition-dependent partitioning, nonideal behavior, altered formation/recovery of target, or imperfections in interpreting the public channels. The evidence supports a monotonic empirical volume effect more securely than a universal equilibrium law.

4. Mixing probably affects approach to the standard partition state. The low-mixing batch had essentially the same phase_ratio as the standard repeats but shifted target signal from organic toward aqueous. The difference exceeds nominal HPLC noise and is directionally consistent with incomplete mass transfer. It is suggestive rather than conclusive because low mixing was tested once and both speed and duration changed together.

5. The separation operation genuinely selects a phase rather than merely relabeling the sample. Complementary organic- and aqueous-retention results support this interpretation. Approximate, rather than exact, pre/post agreement indicates sampling noise, instrument differences, phase entrainment, or composition changes during separation.

Conjecture and competing explanations

A plausible account is that each solvent–extractant combination establishes its own effective affinity and mass-transfer environment; phase volumes then convert that affinity into the observed allocation, while mixing controls how closely the system approaches its settled state. This is a mechanistic conjecture, not an identified molecular explanation, because all materials are anonymous and no structural or property information was supplied.

Material effects could alternatively arise from pairing-specific changes in target production, degradation, impurity formation, phase volumes, or analytical response rather than partition affinity alone. The volume experiment coupled extractant, solvent, and aqueous additions, so it did not isolate a pure volume-ratio effect. The high-extractant batch also had higher impurity signal and lower purity, consistent with a composition change beyond simple redistribution. Likewise, the low-mixing result could reflect batch variability or kinetics unrelated to interphase transfer.

Scope remains limited: all complete material comparisons were one-factor contrasts around S0/X0, not a full 4×4 factorial screen, so most solvent–extractant interactions are unknown. Only two selected standard conditions were replicated; the extreme-volume and low-mixing conditions were not. Mixing speed and duration were confounded, settling time was fixed, and no time series established equilibrium. Predictions are therefore defensible mainly within the tested materials, vessel scale, reagent loading, phase ranges, and settling protocol; extrapolation to unseen pairings or substantially different compositions should carry high uncertainty.

payload.rationale: Predictions interpolate the measured phase-volume trend and pairing contrasts, using the close S0/X3 and S3/X0 repeats to separate signal from instrument noise. X3 shifted substantially more target to organic than X0 with S0, so Q06 exceeds Q05; Q01’s small organic share and weaker S0/X0 affinity leave most target aqueous. Intervals widen for untested S2/X3 interactions and mixing extrapolations, and represent structural/process uncertainty rather than random HPLC noise.

payload.report:
1. No instance prior was supplied: the material dossier contained only anonymous labels and explicitly gave no property estimates. The weakest self-developed assumption was that solvent and extractant effects could be extrapolated approximately independently to unseen pairings. In particular, the high organic predictions for S2/X3 (Q08, Q11, Q12) relied on an untested interaction. The campaign varied all extractants only with S0 and all solvents only with X0, so it never established a separable pairing law. A universal constant partition coefficient was also not supported: batches 4, 8, 10, and 11 gave materially different apparent coefficients across phase compositions.

2. I would run S2/X3 directly at the Q08 amounts and high-mixing conditions, then measure pre-separation HPLC product-in-organic, product-in-aqueous, phase_ratio, purity, and impurity signal. This tests the largest extrapolation while holding the phase recipe equal to Q05–Q08. An organic fraction near 0.7, with approximately conserved total target and no large impurity change, would strengthen the explanation that the observed S2 and X3 effects combine into a strong effective organic affinity. A result near the S2/X0 or S0/X3 levels—or outside both—would show a substantial pairing interaction and invalidate the separable extrapolation. A reduced target sum accompanied by increased impurity would instead favor composition-dependent target loss or transformation over simple redistribution.

3. The purity, impurity, and imperfect mass-closure evidence was underused. Batch 10 combined high organic allocation with impurity 0.076 and purity 0.882, unlike the cleaner standard S0/X3 repeats. The aqueous-retained batch 8 final assay also showed impurity 0.181 and purity 0.732, much different from its pre-separation HPLC values. Identical-volume standard batches additionally showed phase_ratio variation from roughly 0.17 to 0.22, which could contribute to apparent material contrasts.

The least reliable predictions are Q08, Q11, and Q12 because S2/X3 was never tested and their intervals depend on an unknown interaction; Q11–Q12 add unsupported mixing-speed extrapolation. The Q09–Q10 distinction is also weak because only one very-low-mixing condition, batch 12, was observed, with duration and speed confounded.

There is a real modeling tension between the sealed report and predictions. The report emphasized imperfect closure, composition-dependent apparent partitioning, and failure of a universal coefficient, whereas the predictions imposed exactly complementary aqueous and organic fractions and used smooth interpolation plus an implicit separable extrapolation for S2/X3. That simplification was useful for producing points but is more restrictive than the evidence justified and likely made some intervals too confident. This is a present audit of the sealed outputs, not a claim that it was recorded contemporaneously.
